questions.topic: Vaccination clinic staffing becomes routine filling mid-shift
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy schedules one pharmacist with six appropriately licensed support workers exclusively for a vaccination clinic under the Board's 2026-02 temporary expanded supervision ratio. During the clinic, the manager directs tw
questions.legal_decision: Stop expanded-ratio routine filling until staff assignments match ordinary permitted ratio.
questions.critical_exception: The 1:6 ratio is limited to qualifying vaccination services, not mixed routine prescription-filling duties.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If only a compliant 1:4 or 1:3 support roster actually fills prescriptions, the ordinary filling ratio can be met.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy schedules one pharmacist with six appropriately licensed support workers exclusively for a vaccination clinic under the Board's 2026-02 temporary expanded supervision ratio. During the clinic, the manager directs two of the workers to begin routine outpatient prescription filling, leaving the same six-person staffing arrangement in place. No second pharmacist or staffing waiver is available. What should the pharmacist do?

choices.text: Keep the six-to-one ratio because a vaccination service remains open somewhere in the building.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 2026-02 expanded 1:6 ratio is conditioned on the vaccination-service workflow; it does not authorize ordinary prescription filling by the expanded six-person team.

choices.text: Allow the technicians to fill but suspend all counseling until the clinic closes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Withholding counseling does not cure a staffing ratio violation.

choices.text: Reassign work or add pharmacist coverage so the support workers filling prescriptions comply with the ordinary applicable supervisory ratio.
choices.why: Correct. Under Policy 2026-02 §I, ordinary filling activities require the 1:3 or 1:4 ratio conditions instead of relying on the 1:6 vaccination exception.

choices.text: Require all six support workers to obtain CPR training; this alone converts routine filling into vaccination staffing.
choices.why: Incorrect. CPR credentials do not determine which supervisory ratio applies to routine prescription filling.

choices.text: Have the pharmacist supervise remotely from home while the six workers complete all prescription processing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Nothing in the expanded clinic ratio removes the on-premises pharmacist supervision requirement for routine filling.

questions.topic: Intern consultation requires active preceptor presence despite same-building location
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy intern begins counseling a patient on a potentially high-risk drug change. The licensed supervising pharmacist is physically elsewhere in the pharmacy reviewing invoices, cannot contemporaneously observe or hear the
questions.legal_decision: Provide active pharmacist direction throughout high-risk counseling.
questions.critical_exception: Being in the same building is not necessarily active consultation supervision.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist were actively available and observing or directing the consultation, the identified supervision failure would be removed.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy intern begins counseling a patient on a potentially high-risk drug change. The licensed supervising pharmacist is physically elsewhere in the pharmacy reviewing invoices, cannot contemporaneously observe or hear the consultation, and is not monitoring it virtually. A second licensed pharmacist is on-site and available. Which actions are appropriate under Board Policy 2026-02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Allow the intern to complete the consultation independently because the assigned preceptor is somewhere in the building.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section II(C) requires a preceptor actively present in person or virtually for patient or practitioner consultation with material patient-safety implications.

choices.text: Arrange active in-person or virtual pharmacist supervision of the consultation before it proceeds.
choices.why: Correct. Contemporaneous direction or observation by a qualified supervising pharmacist is required for this patient-facing high-risk counseling.

choices.text: Treat the intern's license alone as authority for unsupervised pharmacist-level consultation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Intern licensure does not eliminate direct supervision requirements.

choices.text: Have the available second pharmacist assume and actively provide appropriate direct supervision if the original preceptor cannot.
choices.why: Correct. Policy §II expressly permits a different on-site pharmacist to provide direct supervision when the original preceptor is unavailable.

choices.text: Record counseling as completed by a fully licensed independent pharmacist without changing the actual supervisory arrangements.
choices.why: Incorrect. Documentation does not substitute for required active supervision and must not misrepresent the personnel performing the service.

questions.topic: Senior pharmacy technician asks to independently release prescription on pharmacist break
questions.trigger: A retail pharmacy's only pharmacist is still on the premises but temporarily unavailable for final dispensing review. A licensed certified technician has entered the prescription correctly, resolved no clinical issue, and prepared a labeled
questions.legal_decision: Do not release any unvalidated patient prescription from a technician.
questions.critical_exception: Even when a pharmacist is in the building, a technician cannot substitute for pharmacist final review.
questions.counterfactual_flip: Once a licensed pharmacist completes final dispensing validation, the verified prepared prescription may proceed under lawful handoff arrangements.
questions.stem: A retail pharmacy's only pharmacist is still on the premises but temporarily unavailable for final dispensing review. A licensed certified technician has entered the prescription correctly, resolved no clinical issue, and prepared a labeled patient package. The prescriber is properly registered; the pharmacist has NOT yet performed final validation for this prescription. The patient has an urgent ride home. What is the legally appropriate action?

choices.text: Hold the prescription for pharmacist final validation rather than allow the technician to independently release it.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.04(1) assigns final dispensing process validation to a licensed pharmacist; the technician's certification and urgency do not confer that authority.

choices.text: Release it after the technician signs the pharmacist's initials and promises a later clinical review.
choices.why: Incorrect. Impersonation and retrospective signoff cannot replace pharmacist final validation.

choices.text: Convert the prescription to a verbal order to avoid final validation while the pharmacist is away.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing the transmission format does not remove the professional validation requirement.

choices.text: Have a cashier independently check accuracy and issue the medication on behalf of the pharmacist.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cashier lacks the required professional role to validate and release a new prescription.

choices.text: Allow release because any prescription from a verified prescriber is automatically considered pharmacist-validated.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescriber authenticity is a separate requirement from pharmacist final validation.

questions.topic: Schedule II perpetual inventory: technician data entry versus discrepancy adjustment
questions.trigger: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, a licensed certified pharmacy technician receives an invoiced Schedule II shipment and can correctly enter the documented receipt into the perpetual inventory. A later mandatory physical count shows an unexplain
questions.legal_decision: Separate permitted CII entry from discrepancy investigation and inventory adjustment authorization.
questions.critical_exception: An unexplained discrepancy is not automatically a confirmed reportable theft; investigation is required.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the MOR had completed investigation and made the supported adjustment personally, the specific unauthorized-adjustment defect would not exist.
questions.stem: At a Massachusetts pharmacy, a licensed certified pharmacy technician receives an invoiced Schedule II shipment and can correctly enter the documented receipt into the perpetual inventory. A later mandatory physical count shows an unexplained shortage. The Manager of Record (MOR) has not investigated; a technician proposes changing the perpetual balance to match the shelf count and closing the discrepancy. Which steps comply with 247 CMR 9.21(8)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The certified technician may make permitted entries documenting legitimate Schedule II transactions, subject to required controls.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(8)(f) permits a certified pharmacy technician to make entries into the perpetual inventory.

choices.text: The technician may independently write off the unexplained shortage as shrinkage to reconcile the system.
choices.why: Incorrect. Inventory adjustments stemming from a discrepancy are limited to the MOR or, when absent, an authorized pharmacist designee who reports to the MOR.

choices.text: The MOR must investigate the discrepancy and determine any significant-loss or suspected-theft reporting obligations.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(8)(c) assigns discrepancy investigation and applicable reporting to the MOR.

choices.text: A cashier may correct the count if the technician countersigns after closing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.21(8)(e) prohibits unlicensed personnel from making any entry or adjustment.

choices.text: An adjustment for the discrepancy must be made only by the MOR or the permitted pharmacist designee in the MOR's absence.
choices.why: Correct. This is the specific adjustment rule in 9.21(8)(d).

questions.citation: 247 CMR 9.21(8)(a)–(f); Board Policy 2026-01 where a loss is confirmed

questions.topic: Board investigation demands signed technician delegation records kept by MOR
questions.trigger: During an unannounced Massachusetts pharmacy inspection, a Board investigator requests a current roster of all licensed technician categories, written descriptions of delegated technician duties, and each category's scope of responsibility.
questions.legal_decision: Supply mandated workforce delegation records on request.
questions.critical_exception: Staff badges alone do not describe delegated roles or provide the required roster.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy maintained and produced the specified current written documents, the requested documentation condition would be satisfied.
questions.stem: During an unannounced Massachusetts pharmacy inspection, a Board investigator requests a current roster of all licensed technician categories, written descriptions of delegated technician duties, and each category's scope of responsibility. The MOR has no such documents and says staff badges alone should satisfy the request. Which response is required?

choices.text: Provide badges only; a roster and delegation descriptions are optional when the staff already passed a national exam.
choices.why: Incorrect. National examination status does not replace the documentation duties in 247 CMR 8.06(1).

choices.text: Ask the investigator to return after the next annual pharmacy license renewal before providing employment information.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation requires these records to be available to the Board upon request.

choices.text: Have the unlicensed store cashier author an oral inventory of staff responsibilities with no written record.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 8.06(1) expressly requires a written description of delegated duties and scopes of responsibility.

choices.text: Prepare and provide the current personnel list and written delegated-duty/scope descriptions required of the MOR.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.06(1)(a)–(c) requires these documents to be made available to the Board upon request.

choices.text: Tell the Board that only controlled-substance perpetual inventory records are relevant to an inspection.
choices.why: Incorrect. Board inspection authority includes required personnel-related practice records.

questions.topic: 2026 computer-only trainee classification changes when entering fill workflow
questions.trigger: A pharmacy posts a licensed trainee on its approved schedule for a two-hour computer-based learning module. During the first hour the trainee does not process or support prescriptions. In the second hour, without updating work assignments,
questions.legal_decision: Recalculate the true support ratio as soon as computer-only and dedicated training status change.
questions.critical_exception: A previously printed schedule does not override actual professional tasks performed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the trainee remained exclusively on computer modules and the trainer performed only dedicated supervision, the exclusions could remain under the applicable policy.
questions.stem: A pharmacy posts a licensed trainee on its approved schedule for a two-hour computer-based learning module. During the first hour the trainee does not process or support prescriptions. In the second hour, without updating work assignments, the trainee begins labeling actual patient prescriptions while the dedicated trainer also fills unrelated orders. Which statements follow from Board Policy 2026-02? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The trainee never counts in the staffing ratio for the entire shift because the schedule originally said 'computer training'.
choices.why: Incorrect. A trainee's exclusion applies only during exclusively computer training with no professional capacity assisting the pharmacist.

choices.text: Once the trainee assists with actual prescription work, the trainee must be counted in the applicable support-personnel ratio.
choices.why: Correct. Section III(A)(3) excludes only exclusive computer-based training; actual filling work is a ratio-counted activity.

choices.text: A dedicated trainer remains excluded while independently filling unrelated prescriptions for other patients.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section III(A)(1)(c) requires counting a trainer who performs duties beyond the dedicated trainer/trainee relationship.

choices.text: The trainee may independently validate the patient's prescription because computer-based modules were completed.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither completion of modules nor a trainee credential confers pharmacist final validation authority.

choices.text: The trainer must also be included when independently supporting the pharmacist outside the designated training relationship.
choices.why: Correct. Under §III(A)(1)(c), a trainer loses the ratio exclusion by independently supporting prescription processing.

questions.topic: Manager of Record resists surprise inspection and records request
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy is open during normal operations when a Board inspector arrives without prior notice and requests records needed for a compliance investigation. The MOR refuses because the Board did not book an appointment and offe
questions.legal_decision: Facilitate inspection and provide requested legal pharmacy records.
questions.critical_exception: Absence of advance appointment does not remove the Board's inspection authority.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If there were no valid Board request for operational records, the particular duty to produce those documents would not yet be triggered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy is open during normal operations when a Board inspector arrives without prior notice and requests records needed for a compliance investigation. The MOR refuses because the Board did not book an appointment and offers to provide only sales summaries instead of the specifically requested relevant records. What is the correct legal response?

choices.text: Demand that the Board obtain written permission from the pharmacy's parent corporation before any unannounced inspection.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.24(1) permits the Board or its designees to inspect licensed pharmacies without notice.

choices.text: Require the Board to wait until the annual pharmacist renewal date before reviewing any operational records.
choices.why: Incorrect. Board examination of pharmacy records is not limited to renewal dates.

choices.text: Provide only the requested sales summary because the pharmacy can unilaterally decide which records the Board is allowed to inspect.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.24(3) requires the pharmacy to provide records requested in connection with inspection or investigation.

choices.text: Offer copies only if inspectors first state a specific violation that has already been proven.
choices.why: Incorrect. Compliance inspections may ascertain whether violations exist; proof of a violation need not precede inspection.

choices.text: Cooperate with the unannounced inspection and provide the documents requested for the investigation.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.24(1),(3) expressly authorizes unannounced inspections and requires requested documents.

questions.topic: Repeat viable environmental action result within 60 days requires microbiologist
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital sterile-compounding pharmacy receives an action-level viable-air finding in its ISO Class 7 buffer room. A second action-level finding is reported 43 days later at the same classified location, with interim remediat
questions.legal_decision: Engage microbiologist and perform longitudinal trend-based remediation for repeated EM findings.
questions.critical_exception: Repeat findings in the same classified area within 60 days trigger engagement even if nonconsecutive.
questions.counterfactual_flip: With no repeat action-level result in the same area inside 60 days, §III(G)'s repeat-trigger would not apply although the first result still needs remediation.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital sterile-compounding pharmacy receives an action-level viable-air finding in its ISO Class 7 buffer room. A second action-level finding is reported 43 days later at the same classified location, with interim remediation already documented. The manager proposes simply resetting the trending spreadsheet and continuing ordinary BUDs because the findings were not on consecutive samples. Which actions are supported by Board Policy 2026-03? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Engage a microbiologist for repeat action-level findings in the same classified area within 60 days even if the results were nonconsecutive.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §III(G) includes consecutive or nonconsecutive repeat results in the same ISO classified area within 60 days.

choices.text: Remove the earlier finding from trend analysis once cleaning has occurred.
choices.why: Incorrect. §III(H) requires longitudinal trends and records of CFUs and organisms.

choices.text: Investigate and document both results as part of environmental control risk assessment and CAPA.
choices.why: Correct. §§III–IV require assessment, root-cause review, and remediation records.

choices.text: Maintain required trend analysis including site-specific CFUs and organism history.
choices.why: Correct. §III(H) expressly requires this monitoring analysis.

choices.text: Treat the 43-day gap as automatically restoring full routine BUDs without repeat EM showing successful remediation.
choices.why: Incorrect. §IV(B) requires repeat sampling demonstrating action levels are below threshold before standard BUDs resume.

questions.topic: Sterile compounding under ISO 7 buffer viable remediation has temporary BUD limits
questions.trigger: A licensed Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy receives a viable action-level environmental monitoring result in its ISO Class 7 buffer room, but not in the ISO Class 5 PEC. It immediately assesses the finding, implements an appropri
questions.legal_decision: Use temporary 24h room temperature / 4d refrigerated BUDs if resuming during ISO7 buffer viable remediation.
questions.critical_exception: Affected buffer room and viable—not nonviable—results; full §V risk controls and Board directions govern.
questions.counterfactual_flip: When repeat EM confirms action levels below the policy limits and remediation is successful, standard BUDs may resume if otherwise justified.
questions.stem: A licensed Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy receives a viable action-level environmental monitoring result in its ISO Class 7 buffer room, but not in the ISO Class 5 PEC. It immediately assesses the finding, implements an appropriate remediation and product-risk plan, schedules repeat sampling, and the Board has not ordered a broader shutdown. Repeat environmental results have NOT yet confirmed recovery. The manager proposes using usual Category 2 refrigerated BUDs during remediation. What is the most defensible decision under Board Policy 2026-03?

choices.text: Use routine long BUDs because the ISO Class 5 PEC itself had no positive sample.
choices.why: Incorrect. Under §V, an affected ISO Class 7 buffer room still triggers temporary BUD limits during permitted remediation compounding.

choices.text: If continued compounding is permitted by the risk assessment, limit all affected CSPs to 24 hours at room temperature or four days refrigerated until proper remediation.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §V, ISO Class 7 Buffer Rooms, imposes these maximum BUDs pending successful remediation, absent contrary Board direction.

choices.text: Use a 30-day refrigerated BUD whenever the manager verbally states there is no patient risk.
choices.why: Incorrect. A verbal assurance does not satisfy §V risk assessment and the specified temporary limits.

choices.text: Discard the EM results because a viable-air finding can never affect room BUD decisions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Viable action levels in a classified buffer room may limit compounding and BUDs under Policy 2026-03.

choices.text: Replace the results with a photograph of the cleanroom and keep standard BUDs without repeat testing.
choices.why: Incorrect. §IV(B) requires repeat EM below action levels to demonstrate proper remediation.

questions.citation: Board Policy 2026-03 §§III(A),(E), IV(B), V (ISO Class 7 Buffer Rooms)

questions.topic: Significant ISO 5 microbial contamination creates recall and prescriber duties
questions.trigger: Environmental monitoring in an ISO Class 5 compounding hood identifies a confirmed 19-CFU excursion. Some CSPs prepared in the affected area have already been dispensed and remain within their assigned BUDs. The manager wants to perform a d
questions.legal_decision: Recall current-BUD CSPs plus surveillance, prescriber outreach, microbiologist and remediation.
questions.critical_exception: ISO 5 viable excursion >15 CFU qualifies as significant loss of control, not merely a routine ISO7 action.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an action-level result was confined to an ISO7 anteroom and ISO5 remained controlled, the automatic >15 ISO5 significant-loss recall rule would not apply.
questions.stem: Environmental monitoring in an ISO Class 5 compounding hood identifies a confirmed 19-CFU excursion. Some CSPs prepared in the affected area have already been dispensed and remain within their assigned BUDs. The manager wants to perform a deep clean, avoid notifying prescribers, and wait for patient complaints before investigating previous doses. What actions are required by Massachusetts Board Policy 2026-03? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Dispense remaining in-date CSPs from the affected area because a BUD is a guarantee of sterility.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy treats >15 CFU in ISO 5 as significant loss of control; an assigned BUD does not waive recall or remediation duties.

choices.text: Recall implicated CSPs that remain within their BUDs following a significant ISO Class 5 loss of control.
choices.why: Correct. §III(C) expressly requires recall of CSPs within BUDs for >15 CFU ISO 5 excursion.

choices.text: Conduct adverse-event surveillance and contact the relevant prescribers.
choices.why: Correct. The same §III(C) requires adverse-event surveillance and prescriber contact.

choices.text: Engage a microbiologist and investigate/remediate the affected ISO Class 5 environment.
choices.why: Correct. §III(C), §IV and the general environmental policy impose microbiologist engagement and remediation.

choices.text: Return to standard Category 2 BUDs immediately after surface cleaning, without repeat EM.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy §IV(B) requires demonstrated successful repeat monitoring to resume ordinary BUDs.

questions.topic: Nonviable particle action level: cannot use viable BUD exception to keep compounding
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts compounding pharmacy's ISO Class 7 secondary engineering control fails the action-level NONVIABLE particle count. Staff immediately establish a remediation plan, but the affected classified rooms have not been fully remediat
questions.legal_decision: Suspend affected sterile compounding on nonviable action result until remediated and recertified.
questions.critical_exception: §V temporary viable BUDs do not substitute for nonviable-action full remediation and recertification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the result instead were a viable action level and §V requirements were met, limited compounding with temporary BUDs could be considered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts compounding pharmacy's ISO Class 7 secondary engineering control fails the action-level NONVIABLE particle count. Staff immediately establish a remediation plan, but the affected classified rooms have not been fully remediated or recertified. A supervisor argues that the pharmacy can continue compounding with the temporary 24-hour BUD used for some VIABLE microbial excursions. What is the correct distinction?

choices.text: Continue any Category 2 production as long as the ISO Class 5 hood has passed its last gloved fingertip test.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy imposes an affected-area suspension and recertification requirement for nonviable particle action levels.

choices.text: Reclassify the excursion as viable because viable-results rules permit temporary BUDs.
choices.why: Incorrect. The type of environmental failure must be interpreted accurately; the viable pathway does not override §III(D).

choices.text: Use only a shortened BUD and skip any recertification if the product is urgently needed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy explicitly requires full remediation and recertification for action-level nonviable particle counts unless the Board directs otherwise.

choices.text: Suspend compounding in the affected operation until full remediation and recertification of classified areas, unless the Board directs otherwise.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2026-03 §III(D) treats nonviable particulate action levels differently from the limited viable remediation pathway.

choices.text: Change the sample date in the record and treat the result as no longer actionable.
choices.why: Incorrect. Falsifying records does not satisfy environmental monitoring and reporting requirements.

questions.topic: Defective simple nonsterile compound dispensed: recall without automatic seven-day Board defective-report trigger
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispensed a patient-specific SIMPLE nonsterile compounded cream. Later laboratory testing establishes a harmful potency defect; patients have not reported a serious adverse event, and the preparation is no
questions.legal_decision: Recall defective simple CNSP and log; distinguish specific Board defect report scope.
questions.critical_exception: Dispensed simple CNSP, no suspected serious adverse drug event, not complex category.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the compounded product were sterile or classified as complex CNSP, Policy 2024-04's seven-day Board defective-preparation notification would apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispensed a patient-specific SIMPLE nonsterile compounded cream. Later laboratory testing establishes a harmful potency defect; patients have not reported a serious adverse event, and the preparation is not classified as complex nonsterile. The pharmacy immediately identifies another patient who received the same preparation. Does Board Policy 2024-04 permit waiting for an adverse event before acting, and does its seven-day defective-preparation report automatically apply?

choices.text: Wait until a patient develops serious injury because a simple nonsterile preparation is excluded from all recall rules.
choices.why: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.112 §39D(e) and Policy 2024-04 require immediate recall whenever a compounded preparation may be defective.

choices.text: Keep distributing the stock and submit only a normal CQI report, because the pharmacy is not a sterile compounder.
choices.why: Incorrect. Compounded defective products already dispensed trigger recall obligations regardless of sterility category.

choices.text: Report every simple nonsterile defect to DEA Form 106 within one business day and dispense unaffected-looking units.
choices.why: Incorrect. DEA Form 106 concerns theft/significant loss, and a simple CNSP defect is not automatically reportable under this policy's seven-day Board defect rule.

choices.text: Keep the remaining compounded stock available but email recipients when a complaint arrives.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy requires segregation, no further dispensing, and immediate recipient contact upon recall.

choices.text: Immediately recall and quarantine the defect, contact recipients and maintain the defective-drug log; the policy's seven-day defect report is specific to CSPs or complex CNSPs.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2024-04 and §39D(e) require immediate recall and appropriate records for any defective dispensed compound, whereas its specific seven-day Board report covers defective CSPs and complex-category CNSPs.

questions.topic: Defective compounded preparation discovered before dispensing
questions.trigger: A pharmacy's pharmacist identifies an out-of-specification compounded nonsterile batch during an internal quality check before any part has been dispensed or distributed. The batch remains secured within the pharmacy. There is no patient ex
questions.legal_decision: Hold undistributed defective compound; CQI documentation recommended; no automatic defective-CSP Board report.
questions.critical_exception: No compounded product dispensed; no SADE; no other report triggers.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an affected preparation had already been dispensed, the immediate recall/recipient notification and applicable Board defective-preparation report obligations would change.
questions.stem: A pharmacy's pharmacist identifies an out-of-specification compounded nonsterile batch during an internal quality check before any part has been dispensed or distributed. The batch remains secured within the pharmacy. There is no patient exposure or suspected serious adverse drug event. Which actions are supported by Board Policy 2024-04? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Prevent dispensing of the out-of-specification preparation and correct or dispose of it lawfully as appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Product integrity requires withholding defective material from patient distribution.

choices.text: Contact all patients to announce a product recall even though no patient has received any batch unit.
choices.why: Incorrect. The mandatory recipient recall/contact pathway presupposes dispensed or distributed affected drug preparations.

choices.text: Automatically submit the seven-day Board defective-drug notification because the batch was compounded, regardless of distribution status.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2024-04 specifically says defects discovered before dispensing do not need to be reported through that Board form.

choices.text: Continue dispensing if the product's original calculated BUD has not passed.
choices.why: Incorrect. A computed BUD does not override confirmed potency or quality failure.

choices.text: Document this pre-dispensing event in the pharmacy's CQI process as recommended; the Board's specific defective-preparation form is not mandatory for that undistributed batch.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2024-04 specifically recommends CQI documentation for defects found before dispensing and says these events do not need Board defective-drug reporting.

questions.topic: DSCSA illegitimate drug confirmation: 24-hour notification after investigation
questions.trigger: A pharmacy has quarantined a suspicious prescription-drug shipment and investigated it with the manufacturer. The manufacturer verifies that several packages are counterfeit; the pharmacy has determined the product is illegitimate. Records
questions.legal_decision: Confirm illegitimate product, notify FDA/trading partners within 24h, prevent dispensing and disposition.
questions.critical_exception: Counterfeit verified; this is beyond merely a suspect product awaiting investigation.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If investigation reliably cleared the shipment as legitimate, §582(d)(4)(B)'s confirmed-illegitimate notification rule would not be triggered.
questions.stem: A pharmacy has quarantined a suspicious prescription-drug shipment and investigated it with the manufacturer. The manufacturer verifies that several packages are counterfeit; the pharmacy has determined the product is illegitimate. Records show some units were already transferred to an immediate trading partner, and unshipped units remain quarantined. The team proposes waiting for a wholesaler's monthly meeting before reporting. Under FD&C Act §582(d)(4), which steps are appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Notify FDA and immediate trading partners believed to have received the illegitimate product within 24 hours of that determination.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(B)(ii) requires notification to FDA and immediate partners likely to have received the product not later than 24 hours after the illegitimacy determination.

choices.text: Disposition the illegitimate products under pharmacy control and assist affected trading partners with disposition as required.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(B)(i) imposes these controls and cooperation duties.

choices.text: Release the quarantine because the manufacturer confirmed the product's identity as counterfeit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Confirmation of illegitimacy demands disposition, not release into patient dispensing stock.

choices.text: Keep required investigation and disposition records for the applicable federal retention period.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(A)(iv) requires suspect investigation records for at least six years after conclusion; associated illegitimate-product records remain subject to applicable record requirements.

choices.text: Notify FDA only when a patient reports an injury; confirmed counterfeit stock by itself requires no notification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statutory notification trigger is the determination of illegitimacy, not a patient harm report.

questions.topic: DSCSA product delivered without required trace records: obtain documentation before acceptance
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a new bulk shipment of covered prescription drugs from its usual licensed wholesale distributor. Shipping boxes are intact, but the distributor has provided no required DSCSA product tracing informat
questions.legal_decision: Resolve missing required transaction documentation before treating shipment as eligible saleable inventory.
questions.critical_exception: No special federal small-dispenser tracing exemption applies to this transaction and no evidence of counterfeiting established.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a valid transaction-specific exemption removed the particular tracing obligation and authenticity checks were satisfied, document receipt under that exemption instead.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives a new bulk shipment of covered prescription drugs from its usual licensed wholesale distributor. Shipping boxes are intact, but the distributor has provided no required DSCSA product tracing information, and no applicable transaction exemption applies. Management says the pharmacy can permanently accept the product into saleable stock because the seller is trusted and supply is short. What is the best first compliance action?

choices.text: Accept the shipment without tracing documents because the supplier has a current distributor license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Trading-partner authorization and product-tracing documentation are separate obligations under §582(d)(1).

choices.text: Add an invented trace record showing a typical manufacturer and release all units.
choices.why: Incorrect. Fabricated records cannot substitute for required tracing information and undermine supply-chain integrity.

choices.text: Obtain the required tracing information from the trading partner and hold release until its receipt and legitimacy are appropriately established.
choices.why: Correct. FD&C Act §582(d)(1)(A) requires required transaction documentation with ownership transfer, and FDA advises dispensers to work with trading partners to obtain missing documents.

choices.text: Treat every missing invoice automatically as proof of an illegitimate counterfeit requiring a 24-hour notice.
choices.why: Incorrect. Missing transaction documentation must be resolved; it does not by itself prove the separate 'illegitimate product' notification threshold.

choices.text: Ignore the missing records for six years because trace documentation is required only after a pharmacy resells the medicine.
